claims.text: High-entropy alloys comprise five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The starting nanoparticles are chemically disordered, single-phase FCC or BCC solid solutions.
Structural and chemical stability is governed by a temperature-dependent competition between configurational entropy and pairwise mixing enthalpy.
At high temperature, configurational entropy lowers the free energy of disordered solid-solution phases and makes ordered compounds less competitive.
Near-zero or balanced pairwise mixing enthalpies allow configurational entropy to sustain one disordered solid solution throughout 473–1923 K.
At low temperature, favorable ordering enthalpy can overcome the configurational-entropy contribution.
Strongly negative pairwise mixing enthalpy can induce chemical ordering or phase separation as temperature decreases.
Low-temperature enthalpic effects can precipitate intermetallic secondary phases.
Ni–Si is an example of a strongly negative mixing-enthalpy pair relevant to the proposed transition.
The local FCC or BCC atomic arrangement modulates the interplay between diffusion kinetics and mixing enthalpy.
Systems with balanced pairwise interactions remain chemically disordered as temperature decreases.
Nanoparticles with balanced pairwise interactions will retain their initial single phase and uniform elemental distribution.
Nanoparticles containing strongly negative mixing-enthalpy pairs will develop more ordering, segregation, or secondary phases than balanced-interaction controls.
Ordering or secondary-phase formation should be especially evident near 473 K.
The controlled comparison should change alloy composition by including or avoiding strongly negative mixing-enthalpy pairs while otherwise treating the nanoparticle groups identically.
The comparison is to be conducted under inert or controlled atmosphere while cycling between 473 K and 1923 K.
Oxidation, reactive environments, or extreme pressure can independently alter phase stability and confound the entropy–enthalpy mechanism.
The exact transition temperature and the mixing-enthalpy threshold required for ordering or phase separation are not defined.
Failure of the negative-mixing-enthalpy group to show any additional ordering or phase separation, or identical phase behavior in both groups over the full cycle, would falsify the hypothesis.
